https://www.fingerlakes1.com/2026/07/26/.text: Home » News » Woman pleads guilty in deadly St. Lawrence River smuggling case Woman pleads guilty in deadly St. Lawrence River smuggling case July 26, 2026 8:59 AM Staff Report A dual Canadian American citizen pleaded guilty to federal charges for organizing a human smuggling attempt that ended with five deaths when a boat capsized in severe weather on the St. Lawrence River in 2023. Stephanie Square, 53, of the Akwesasne Mohawk Indian Territory in Canada, admitted to conspiracy to commit human smuggling, four counts of smuggling for financial gain and four counts of smuggling resulting in death, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of New York. Federal prosecutors said Square led a smuggling organization that regularly moved people across the U.S.-Canada border through Akwesasne. During the week of March 27, 2023, she was contacted about moving a Romanian family of four, including two children younger than 3, across the river into the United States. According to court documents, one person declined to help because of high winds. Prosecutors said Square continued the operation despite high winds, freezing temperatures and limited visibility because she expected to be paid. The family was taken to Timothy Oakes' residence on Cornwall Island early March 29 and later brought to a boat launch, prosecutors said. Casey Oakes attempted to pilot the family across the river that night, but the boat capsized in severe weather. The bodies of the four family members were recovered March 30 and 31 along with the boat. Casey Oakes' body was found eight months later. Square is scheduled to be sentenced Nov. 25. She faces a mandatory minimum of five years in prison and a maximum sentence of life, though a federal judge will determine the sentence after reviewing federal guidelines and other factors. Five other co-conspirators have pleaded guilty in the case, including two people who were extradited from Canada. Homeland Security Investigations in Massena led the investigation with assistance from U.S., Canadian, state, local and tribal agencies. https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/141252.text: Hungary bus crash kills 12 Polish pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina Hungarian police said the bus crashed near Mezőkeresztes on the M3 motorway at around 1:00 AM Twelve people have been killed after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims overturned on a motorway in Hungary while returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Hungarian police said the bus crashed near Mezőkeresztes on the M3 motorway at around 1:00 AM local time after it “went off the straight road into a ditch and overturned”. Early reports suggested the driver may have fallen asleep. He survived and was taken into custody as authorities investigate the cause of the crash. The bus was carrying 57 passengers and two drivers from Poland's south-eastern Podkarpackie region. The group had been returning from a pilgrimage to the Catholic shrine of Međugorje. Poland's foreign ministry said “virtually all” surviving passengers were taken to hospitals in Eger, Debrecen and Miskolc, with 10 people in serious condition. Hungary's ambulance service said another 37 suffered minor injuries. “With deep sorrow, I received the tragic news of the accident involving a Polish bus in Hungary, in which so many of our compatriots perished,” Polish President Karol Nawrocki said. Polish prosecutors from Krosno will lead an investigation into the crash. Poland's infrastructure minister also announced enhanced inspections of buses and drivers' working hours following the tragedy. https://www.tmz.com/2026/09/10/adrian-sz.text: "Married at First Sight" star Adrian Szymaniak has sadly died at 39 ... a year after he was diagnosed with stage 4 cancer. Adrian, who was an alum of the Polish version of the show, suffered from a brain tumor before his death. His wife, Anita, broke the news on Instagram, writing ... "With great pain we inform that Adrian has passed away. In these extremely difficult moments, what matters most to us is silence, closeness and the chance to say goodbye to him among those nearest to him." The couple met on the third season of the show before tying the knot in 2018 ... and welcoming two kids. Adrian -- who renewed his vows with Anita this past December -- shared his cancer journey on Instagram. He previously wrote ... Ryan De Nino -- who joined the show on season 2, where he married Jessica Castro -- died in August. Ryan, who later divorced from Jessica, was 40. RIP

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c69w.text: Figure caption, Watch: Why are students staging protests at schools in France? By Hugh Schofield Paris correspondent Published 4 hours ago It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble. Since the student protests of May 1968 â memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) â every government has run scared of angry French youth. Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in. Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away. For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colÃ¨re (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed. Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats". A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country. Live: Fires lit on streets across France after student protests force hundreds of schools to close On Thursday â the high point so far â hundreds of lycÃ©es (where 15-18 year-olds finish their schooling) were being blockaded. On Friday, the situation had improved but around 400 lycÃ©es were closed in order to protect staff and students. Universities are beginning to join in. Violence has erupted. On Thursday the main hall of a lycÃ©e in Nantes was destroyed by fire. Smaller fires too numerable to mention were lit at school entrance gates around the country. The cost of the damage is millions of euros. According to Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray, 65 teaching staff including 40 school heads have been injured. "Most of the staff who were hurt said that the people they were facingâ¦ were not their own pupils," he said. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Since the infamous protests of 1968, French governments have known the power of young people taking to the streets In addition, the government says that around 300 police and firefighters have been treated for injuries, and some 2,000 people â mainly minors â taken into custody. For their part, student groups say they have a long list of people injured by police. Two teenagers have serious eye injuries and one has lost many of his teeth. The problem would be hard enough if it was just a question of meeting the protesters' demands. But there is another dimension â a political and social one â which makes this student crisis far more dangerous than in the past. The demands do exist, even if they remain vague. They are about money â the lack of it â and the need for more teachers, smaller classes and better buildings. On such matters, many in France would agree with the teenagers. Certainly using protest to demand money from government is such a national habit that even governments agree it's legitimate. And of course, things are indeed getting worse in the education system â because money is so tight. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The protests have spread across France, and some university students are now joining in This week Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu published his draft for next year's budget. The motif is "More cuts â and this time we're serious!" Whether or not he manages to remove â¬54bn (Â£46bn) from state spending, as he promises, remains open to question. But it is surely obvious that the era of public largesse to defuse social unrest in France is now in its twilight. Students demanding an extra school nurse or insulation in the dining-block are likely to be disappointed. But that is the lesser of the worries. The far greater fear is that these student protests are being manipulated by the hard left â and that the violence of recent days is a foretaste of what awaits a dangerously polarised society in the year of elections that is coming. For the right and centre, there is no doubt that behind the student trouble lies the cunning hand of the France Unbowed party (LFI) and its popular presidential candidate, Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon. LFI leaders have regularly appeared next to the students â notably in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis whose mayor Bally Bagayoko was criticised for saying that "violence can sometimes be legitimate." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bally Bagayoko (left) and presidential candidater Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon (right) have supported the right of the students to protest An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unionsâ¦ and political groups such asâ¦ LFI." It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategyâ¦ aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections". In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycÃ©ens , the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics â like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook. The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday MÃ©lenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests". But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran â who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen â knows exactly what he is doing. Polls show he has massive support â some 40% -- among 18-24 year-olds in France, and that this is concentrated in the populous, high-immigration city suburbs where his talk of a "new France" and "creolisation", to reflect France's changing language and population, are highly appreciated. But young people are also the biggest abstainers in French elections, so the strategy â as the elections approach â will be to give constant reminders to this part of the population that the LFI is at their side, and that their vote can count. Whether this will be enough to ensure victory for MÃ©lenchon is another matter. He must surely take seriously the polls which all show him losing massively in a run-off against Le Pen. If that happens, France will be in very unstable territory - for which the young people's protests of recent days will indeed have been a harbinger. CC Charles Cohen 2026.09.26 08:00 The site where a Russan drone was shot down in Lithuania in September. | D. Umbrasas / LRT Europe has so far avoided accusing Moscow of committing acts of war, writes Charles Cohen for Euractiv, partners of LRT English. Hybrid threats from Moscow are intensifying in pace and scope, but Europeans donât seem to agree on how to label them. Numerous examples illustrate this looming threat. Last week, Belarus held a four-day military drill along the Polish-Lithuanian border as Ukraine reported that Russia was using Belarusian relay stations to guide drone attacks on targets in western Ukraine. That same week, NATO assets shot down a drone coming from Belarus outside the Lithuanian city of Kaunas. Earlier this month, Germany stated that Russia was behind a drone attack targeting Ukrainian cargo planes at the Leipzig/Halle airport in August. âWe are not at war, but we are the target of hybrid warfare every day,â German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said. The EU so far has trodden a careful line, referring to these events as âhybridâ, and not direct acts of war. Hybrid threats differ from armed conflict or hostilities in that they typically remain below the threshold of conventional warfare, a European Commissionâs spokesperson said to Euractiv in writing, pointing to a combination of coercive, subversive, cyber, informational, economic or other non-kinetic and, at times, limited kinetic means in a coordinated manner. The goal, the Commission said, is to exploit statesâ vulnerabilities, âwithout necessarily triggering a formal state of warâ. âWe should be under no illusions about what is happening here: hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats,â Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said during her September address to MEPs in Strasbourg. The recent acts of sabotage and drone incursions are leading some leaders to harden their discourse. Earlier this month, EU High Representative Kaja Kalla said the Leipzig/Halle attack had âall the characteristics of state-sponsored terrorismâ. Last Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told national lawmakers Russia could strike countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland, using drones and missiles and pass them off as accidents. A day later, French President Emmanuel Macron said the ânature of Russian aggression and the threats in Europe are changingâ, after briefing party leaders and presidential candidates on national security ahead of the 2027 elections. The site where a Russan drone was shot down in Lithuania in September. | D. Umbrasas / LRT Whatâs in a word? NATO defines hybrid threats as a combination of military and non-military, as well as covert and overt, means, including disinformation, cyberattacks, economic pressure, deployment of irregular armed groups and use of regular forces. Shortly after von der Leyenâs speech, MEPs endorsed a report calling for a coordinated EU response mechanism against âhybrid threatsâ. âI donât like this title,â Rasa JukneviÄienÄ, the European Peopleâs Party MEP who initiated the report, told Euractiv, pointing to a lack of a better alternative. âIt does not exactly reflect the reality on the ground, because it looks like itâs not a real war.â âWe named those hybrid attacks or hybrid warfare as acts that are not related to each other, but the war that is conducted by Russia involves very concrete people and institutions,â the former Lithuanian defence minister added. The threshold question Russia has so far targeted European countries within what some experts call a âgrey zoneâ, below the threshold that would trigger a conventional response. For some countries, clearly labelling the state of the threat encourages Russia to go further. âThe mere fact that we label it under threshold helps push the boundary of what is acceptable or not,â an Eastern flank official told Euractiv. The source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said their country was differentiating between Russiaâs hybrid or sabotage activities and its military threats towards NATOâs Eastern flank. To better address the Kremlinâs strategy against EU countries, von der Leyen last week proposed a âcounter-hybrid playbookâ as part of the highly anticipated European Security Strategy. The mechanism will help capitals react to âincidentsâ that fall âbelow armed conflict but clearly threaten our national securityâ, the Commission chief said, adding it would resemble NATOâs Article 4. But some argue that too much clarity could serve the Kremlin. For Jamie Shea, a former NATO deputy assistant secretary-general, âbeing too clear about levels of response takes away the ambiguity which is key to deterrence, keeping your opponent guessingâ. The aggressor could then continue provoking and disrupting up to a certain level without worrying about the response, he added. The site where a Russan drone was shot down in Lithuania in September. | D. Umbrasas / LRT Shadow war? Carlo Masala, director of the Centre for Intelligence and Security Studies at the German Armed Forces University in Munich, told Euractiv he would rather âcall it shadow warâ. âFrom the Russian perspective, this is a real war,â Masala said. If one is the daily target of warfare activities, then one is at war even if one is not responding to those attacks, the US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) concluded in a September report on âthe Russian military campaign against Europeâ. While some experts say escalatory war rhetoric could fuel Moscowâs escalation, the ISW argues Europeâs current language constrains Western responses and signals tolerance to Moscow. The multiplication of incidents is also testing the efficiency of Europeâs current deterrence and carries the risk of âunintended escalationâ, Linas Kojala, the head of the Vilnius-based Geopolitics and Security Studies Centre, said. âChanging the narrative from hybrid would not mean we change the type of threat we are facing, because it depends on Russiaâs understanding of the effectiveness of Western deterrence,â he added. Using âshadow warâ instead, Masala said, would not change the threshold but would make it clearer to Europeans that this is âan orchestrated campaign that is similar to a warâ, but with no troops. EU ambassadors are set to discuss Russiaâs hybrid threats when they meet next Wednesday, as the Commission continues drafting its European Security Strategy. Composite: Win McNamee/Getty Images US midterm elections 2026 Senate race in once reliably Republican South Carolina tied in final stretch – poll Democrat Annie Andrews neck-and-neck with Republican incumbent, Darline Graham, sister to Lindsey Graham US politics live – latest updates Joseph Gedeon in Washington Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.42 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A US Senate race in one of the most Republican states in the country is now a dead heat, according to a new poll showing Annie Andrews, a Democrat, tied with Darline Graham, the Republican incumbent senator. South Carolina has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998, and Donald Trump won it by nearly 18 points in 2024, but a New York Times/Siena poll this week has the two candidates neck and neck, at 48% each. Graham was appointed to the seat after her brother, Lindsey Graham, died in July, and she entered the race at Trump’s urging, without having ever held elected office. Her inexperience has become one of the defining aspects of the campaign, which culminated in an August debate when she admitted she was “not that informed on national security” when asked about US policy on Taiwan. In the poll, 51% of voters said she lacked the right experience to be an effective senator. Andrews, a pediatrician from Charleston, has meanwhile built her campaign around her medical career. Her solution to better access to doctors and climbing medical bills has been to advocate for a public option and cheaper prescription drugs. But she has kept her distance from the Democratic party’s left flank, saying she does not support the Medicare for All proposed model of universal healthcare, while also conceding that Democrats failed on the border, and declining to name a national Democrat she would like to campaign with her. That pitch appears to be working with independents, who back her over Graham by 57% to 37%. Graham, by contrast, is leaning heavily on Trump’s support. She opposes abortion rights, and has said she completely trusts Trump on tariffs and the war with Iran. On immigration, she has argued that anyone in the country illegally should be deported “immediately”. Trump visited the state last week to rally for Graham in a 90-minute speech, calling Andrews extreme and drawing repeated interruptions from protesters. He returns again on Thursday. Republicans are spending heavily in South Carolina, despite their longstanding electoral dominance in the state. The party’s establishment is also not entirely united: one Republican congressman, Ralph Norman, who lost the runoff against Graham, has said he will not campaign for her. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly, for twelve weeks Sign up to How We Win Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk. after newsletter promotion Other recent polls show an equally tight contest, though most have Graham narrowly ahead. A South Carolina Policy Council survey conducted this month gave Graham a one-point lead, within its margin of error. That same poll showed how much Andrews has been outrunning her own party – the Democratic candidate for governor, Jermaine Johnson, trailed the Republican, Alan Wilson, by 10 points.
